l: Pharaoh's dream of the grain, Genesis
s: Pharaoh's second dream: seven healthy heads of grain on one stalk are swallowed by seven thin heads blasted by the east wind. Joseph interprets it as the same as the cattle dream, one dream: seven years of plenty followed by seven of famine.

has_duration seven years [in Egypt] Joseph foretells seven years of great plenty throughout Egypt, represented by the good cattle and heads of grain. They come as foretold, and the earth produces abundantly. During them Joseph gathers food, and his two sons are born before the famine. The years then come to an end.

A seven-year famine follows seven years of plenty, which Joseph interprets from the thin cattle and blasted grain. It is very grievous and severe over all the earth, though Egypt alone has bread, and Joseph opens the storehouses to sell grain. As it continues, the grain from Egypt is eaten up, driving the sons back to buy more food so they may live.

Manasseh, Joseph's firstborn son born in Egypt, is named for God making Joseph forget his toil. Jacob claims him as his own like Reuben and Simeon, foretelling he will be a great people, though his younger brother will be greater.

Ephraim, whose name means God has made me fruitful, is Joseph's younger son born in Egypt. Jacob claims him as his own, places his right hand on him, and sets him before Manasseh, foretelling greater offspring and a multitude of nations.

Grain stores in Egypt's cities, filled from surrounding fields under Pharaoh's hand on Joseph's advice, taking a fifth in plentiful years, laying up grain like sea sand until counting stopped; in the famine Joseph opened them and sold grain to Egyptians and all countries.

Joseph's ten brothers are a group who go to Egypt, bow to Joseph without recognizing him, and are accused by him of spying. They protest honesty, privately admit guilt concerning Joseph, then fear finding money in their sacks and report to Jacob.
Grain is bought in Egypt because of the famine, so that Jacob's family may live and not die. Joseph has the brothers' bags filled with it and sends it home for the famine of their houses.

is_located_in grain [brothers' money restored into their sacks] The brothers' payment for grain is secretly restored by Joseph's command into each man's sack. One brother discovers his at the lodging place, and the rest find their bundles of money when they empty their sacks at home, leaving them frightened and asking what God has done to them.

is_made_by Joseph [against his brothers] Joseph accuses the brothers of being spies who have come to see the nakedness of the land, and repeats it when they deny it. He sets a test: one brother stays bound while the rest bring back the youngest, and he says this will verify their words. The brothers deny the charge, and Jacob is told of it on their return.

are_seated_by birthright order [firstborn to youngest] The brothers defend themselves to their father by saying they only answered the man's questions, then go down to Egypt with the present, double money, and Benjamin. Brought to Joseph's house, they fear arrest and enslavement over the returned money and explain themselves to the steward, who reassures them and brings Simeon out. They bow before Joseph, are seated by birthright and age, marvel at it, and drink and are merry with him.

l: money returned in the sacks, Genesis
s: was_attributed_by_steward_to God [steward says God gave them treasure in sacks] The money found in the sacks on the first trip makes Israel suspect an oversight, so he tells his sons to bring it back along with double money. On arrival it makes the brothers fear that Joseph will seek occasion against them and seize them as slaves. They explain it to the steward, who says their God gave them treasure in their sacks and that he received their money.

contains balm, honey, spices, myrrh, nuts, almonds [choice fruits of the land] Israel directs his sons to bring a present of choice fruits of the land: a little balm, honey, spices, myrrh, nuts, and almonds. The brothers prepare it for Joseph's arrival at noon and, when he comes home, bring it into the house and bow to the earth before him.

Joseph's brothers are a group of shepherds who worship their father's God and live in Goshen, granted by Pharaoh. They call themselves Joseph's servants. In Chapter 44 they are accused over a missing cup, found in Benjamin's sack, and fall before Joseph in distress. In Chapter 47 five of them are presented to Pharaoh, state their trade, and are given Goshen and bread during the famine. In Chapter 50, after burying their father, they fear Joseph's revenge, plead for forgiveness, and are comforted, with Joseph promising God will bring them to the promised land.

Joseph's silver cup was secretly put in the mouth of the youngest brother's sack. The steward said Joseph drinks from it and uses it to divine, and it was found in Benjamin's sack, which brought the accusation of theft against the brothers.
Goshen is a land in Egypt proposed as dwelling for Jacob's family; Judah guides them there, Jacob arrives, and Joseph meets him, planning settlement apart from Egyptians who despise shepherds.

l: Joseph's revelation to his brothers, Genesis
s: is_a disclosure of identity [Joseph made himself known] Joseph, unable to restrain himself, sends everyone else out and says "I am Joseph!", leaving his brothers terrified and speechless until he asks them to come near. He reassures them that God, not they, sent him to Egypt to preserve life, after which he weeps, embraces and kisses them, and they talk with him.

l: journey of Jacob's family to Egypt, Genesis
s: Jacob's sons carry him, the children, and wives in Pharaoh's wagons from Beersheba with livestock and goods; all his offspring reach Egypt's Goshen.

l: reunion of Jacob and Joseph, Genesis
s: takes_place_in Goshen Joseph goes up in his chariot to Goshen, presents himself to Israel, falls on his neck, and weeps a good while. Israel says he may now die, having seen that Joseph is still alive.

affects Egypt [also Canaan; very severe] The famine is described as very severe in both Egypt and Canaan, leaving no bread in all the land and causing both lands to faint. It drives Jacob's family to Egypt and exhausts the people's money, then their livestock, and finally their land, leading to the Egyptians' sale of themselves and their fields.

Driven by famine, Joseph buys all Egypt's land for Pharaoh as Egyptians sell their fields, excluding the priests' land since they had a portion from Pharaoh. People are moved to cities and given seed; a fifth of harvests goes to Pharaoh by Joseph's statute.

Jacob's burial instruction is a charge made as his death nears: he asks Joseph to swear not to bury him in Egypt but to carry him to his ancestors' burying place. Joseph swears. Jacob then charges all his sons to bury him with his fathers in the cave of Machpelah, bought by Abraham, and dies after finishing.

l: Jacob's blessing of Ephraim and Manasseh, Genesis
s: Jacob blesses Joseph's sons Ephraim and Manasseh, invoking the God of Abraham and Isaac and asking that they become a multitude. He deliberately crosses his hands, right on younger Ephraim, and over Joseph's protest declares Ephraim greater. He establishes the blessing formula 'God make you as Ephraim and as Manasseh,' placing Ephraim first.

consists_of sons of Jacob [blessed each according to his own blessing] The twelve tribes of Israel are identified as the sons Jacob has just addressed, each described in his own pronouncement. The text says Jacob blessed everyone according to his own blessing.

given_to twelve tribes of Israel [each according to his own blessing] Jacob's blessings are individual pronouncements over each son, some of rebuke and some of praise or promise, concerning what will happen to them. The narrator says he blessed everyone according to his own blessing, and Joseph's blessing is said to prevail above the blessings of Jacob's ancestors.

Burial of Israel (Jacob): a great procession of chariots, horsemen, Egyptian elders and Joseph's family travels, mourns seven days at Atad's threshing floor, named Abel Mizraim, then his sons bury him in Machpelah's cave near Mamre.

Leviticus is a book of laws the LORD gives to Moses for the children of Israel, concluding with the statement that these are the commandments given on Mount Sinai. Its central concern is how a people can live near a holy God: the LORD is holy, so Israel must be holy. The most important figures are the LORD, Moses as mediator, and Aaron and his sons, the priests. The book opens with the offering system: burnt, meal, peace, sin and trespass offerings (chapters 1-5), then the priests' procedures and portions (6-7). Moses consecrates Aaron and his sons with washing, anointing, blood and offerings (8). On the eighth day the LORD's glory appears and fire consumes the offering (9). Soon after, Nadab and Abihu offer strange fire and are devoured; the priests are told to avoid wine at the Tent of Meeting and to distinguish holy from common (10). The focus then moves to purity. Chapters 11-15 cover clean and unclean animals, childbirth, skin disease and mildew in garments and houses, and bodily discharges, with rites of cleansing. Chapter 16 sets out the Day of Atonement: Aaron enters the Most Holy Place, blood is sprinkled on the mercy seat, and a live goat carries Israel's sins into the wilderness. Chapter 17 requires sacrifices to be brought to the Tent of Meeting and forbids eating blood because life is in the blood. Chapters 18-20 address conduct: forbidden sexual relations, Molech worship and mediums, with penalties of death or being cut off, alongside the call to be holy, love one's neighbor and the stranger as oneself, and deal justly. Chapters 21-22 set stricter standards of holiness for priests and for handling holy things. Chapter 23 lists the appointed feasts: Sabbath, Passover, first fruits, the feast of weeks, trumpets, atonement and booths. Chapter 24 covers the lamp, the bread, and the stoning of a man who blasphemed the Name, with laws of equal retribution. Chapter 25 regulates the Sabbath year and the Jubilee, land redemption, and treatment of poor brothers. Chapter 26 gives the covenant of blessings for obedience and escalating curses for disobedience, ending with the promise to remember the covenant with Jacob, Isaac and Abraham if the people confess. Chapter 27 explains valuing and redeeming vows, dedicated things and tithes.

The LORD is the God of the children of Israel, who speaks throughout these records, mostly to Moses and sometimes to Aaron, from the Tent of Meeting and at Mount Sinai. He is holy, and he repeatedly identifies himself as the one who brought Israel out of Egypt, broke the yoke of their slavery, and made them his own people to be their God. What matters most is that he makes Israel holy and separates them from the peoples and from uncleanness, and that he dwells among them in the tabernacle, appearing in the cloud on the mercy seat. The records open with his instructions for offerings: burnt, meal, peace, sin and trespass offerings, which he receives as a pleasant aroma, and he assigns portions to the priests. He then has Aaron and his sons consecrated, all done as he commanded. His glory appears and fire from him consumes the offering. Fire also devours Nadab and Abihu for strange fire he had not commanded. He forbids wine to priests entering the Tent and commands them to distinguish holy from common and clean from unclean. He then gives laws on clean and unclean animals, childbirth, leprosy, mildew, and discharges, followed by rules for the yearly atonement, where Aaron enters the Most Holy Place. Later chapters have him require sacrifices at the Tent of Meeting, forbid eating blood, and command Israel to reject the customs of Egypt and Canaan. He forbids sexual sins and child sacrifice to Molech, sets penalties, and warns he will set his face against and cut off offenders. He says he is casting out the nations and will give Israel the land of Canaan. He gives rules for priestly holiness and sets his feasts, the lamp oil and bread, and the penalty for the blasphemer. He gives the Sabbath year and Jubilee, claiming the land as his. The account closes with covenant blessings for obedience, including walking among Israel, and escalating punishments for disobedience, such as laying waste cities and destroying high places. Even then he promises to remember his covenant with Jacob, Isaac, and Abraham if the people confess and humble themselves, and not to reject them utterly. A final set of rules on vows and dedicated things claims firstborn animals and the tithe as holy to him.

Moses is the human mediator through whom the LORD's laws and commands reach Aaron, his sons, and the children of Israel in Leviticus. Across the records he is called from the Tent of Meeting, receives the LORD's words repeatedly, and relays them: offering rules, laws on fat, blood and peace offerings, dietary laws, discharge laws, conduct and forbidden relations, holiness for priests, and the appointed feasts. The records close by noting that the commandments were given to him on Mount Sinai. Most important is his role as a faithful, commanded agent who acts as the LORD commanded him. He is also a relative of Aaron, whom he addresses as leader of the priests and calls his brother. The account unfolds in stages. In the early chapters (1, 6, 7) he is mainly a recipient and relayer of offering instructions. In Chapter 8 he becomes an active officiant at the ordination: he assembles the congregation, washes and clothes Aaron and his sons, anoints the tabernacle, altar and Aaron, performs the offerings, takes the breast of the ram of consecration as his portion, and instructs them to remain at the door for seven days. In Chapter 9, on the eighth day, he commands the offerings, tells the people the LORD's glory will appear, directs Aaron to make atonement, goes with Aaron into the Tent of Meeting, and blesses the people. In Chapter 10 he interprets the deaths as fulfillment of the LORD's word, has Mishael and Elzaphan carry the bodies out of the camp, instructs Aaron, Eleazar and Ithamar not to mourn openly or leave the Tent, and directs the eating of the offering portions. He feels anger at Eleazar and Ithamar over the burned sin offering goat but is pleased by Aaron's reply. Later chapters (11, 15-19, 21-23, 27) return him to the intermediary role, with Chapter 16 telling Aaron not to enter the Most Holy Place at just any time, and Chapter 23 closing with Moses declaring the feasts. In Chapter 24 the people bring a blasphemer to him; he waits for the LORD's will, then speaks the command, and the people carry out the stoning.

The children of Israel are the people addressed by the LORD through Moses, who previously lived as foreigners in Egypt and are now being brought to Canaan, a land they will inherit as promised. They are called the LORD's people and servants, set apart as his own, and commanded above all to be holy because the LORD is holy. The records open with rules for offerings: livestock from herd or flock, peace offerings with portions for the priests, and a congregation that stands before the LORD, is blessed by Aaron and Moses, and falls on its face when fire consumes the offering. Rules follow on clean and unclean animals, bodily discharges and uncleanness, and the Day of Atonement, when two goats carry away sins and the people afflict their souls and do no work. Sacrifices must be brought to the Tent of Meeting, blood must not be eaten, and sacrifice to goat idols must stop. Central to the whole is separation from the customs of Egypt, Canaan and the nation being cast out: prohibitions on forbidden sexual relations, Molech, idols, mediums and wizards, with penalties and the warning that the land will vomit out those who commit such abominations. Chapter 19 gathers ethical commands: keep Sabbaths, respect mother and father, honor the elderly, revere the sanctuary, leave field corners and gleanings for the poor and foreigner, keep just measures, and love neighbor and stranger as yourself. Later laws cover feasts as holy convocations with rest and shelters remembering the exodus, oil for the lamp and the bread, and the stoning of a blasphemer. In the land they must keep the Sabbath year and Jubilee, deal fairly, redeem relatives' property, lend to the poor without interest, and not treat fellow Israelites harshly or sell them as slaves, since they are the LORD's servants. The account ends with blessing for obedience and severe punishment for rejecting his laws: defeat, scattering among the nations, and fear in enemy lands. Yet if they confess their own and their fathers' iniquity and humble their uncircumcised hearts, the LORD will remember his covenant and not reject them.

Aaron is a priest and the brother of Moses, whose role is set out across the records as the anointed head of a priestly line. He and his sons are consecrated together, anointed with oil, and given a lasting portion from the children of Israel, including the breast of the peace offerings and a share of the twelve cakes and the remainder of the meal offering, eaten in a holy place. He wears the tunic, sash, robe, ephod, the breastplate containing the Urim and Thummim, and a turban with a golden plate. His duties include offering sin offerings and making atonement for himself and the people, blessing the people, keeping the lamp stand in order from evening to morning, distinguishing holy from common and clean from unclean, and teaching Israel the statutes. He is forbidden wine and strong drink when entering the Tent of Meeting, and he is commanded to stay there seven days with his sons. The account unfolds in stages. First come the laws of the offerings and the portion given to Aaron and his sons. Next he is washed, clothed, anointed and sanctified, with blood placed on his right ear, thumb and great toe. Then he carries out the offerings Moses commanded, killing the calf for his own sin offering and then offering the people's offerings, and he blesses the people twice. His sons Nadab and Abihu die when they come near before the LORD. Aaron holds his peace, the LORD speaks to him directly with the prohibition and charge, and when Moses questions the burned sin offering Aaron answers and Moses is satisfied. Eleazar and Ithamar remain as surviving sons. Later he is addressed with Moses on clean and unclean animals and on discharges. He is told how to enter the Most Holy Place, bathed and in holy linen, with a bull and a ram, casting lots for two goats, bringing incense and blood within the veil, atoning for the sanctuary and altar, and confessing Israel's sins over the live goat. The closing units address him as ancestor of the priestly line, whose offspring with a defect may not approach to offer the bread of God, then on separating from holy things and on offerings without defect, and finally on the lamps and the holy bread.

Aaron's sons are the priests, a consecrated group set apart by the LORD to serve at the altar at the Tent of Meeting. Across Leviticus they carry out the sacrificial system: they sprinkle the blood around the altar, put fire on it, lay wood in order, arrange the pieces, and burn the fat and offerings, including birds and herd offerings. In the meal offering the priest burns a memorial handful, and the remainder belongs to Aaron and his sons as a most holy part of the LORD's fire offerings. They eat it unleavened in the court of the Tent of Meeting. Every male among them has a perpetual portion forever throughout their generations, including the waved breast and, for the one who offers the blood and fat of the peace offerings, the right thigh. Whoever touches these portions becomes holy. In Chapter 8 they are washed, clothed by Moses in tunics, sashes and headbands, lay hands on the bull and rams, receive blood on right ear, thumb and great toe, are sprinkled with oil and blood, eat the consecration meal, and remain at the Tent of Meeting seven days. Holiness is the central demand. They must be holy to their God and not profane his name: no shaving heads or beards, cutting flesh, defiling themselves for the dead beyond near relatives, or marrying a prostitute, profane woman or divorced woman. A priest's daughter who profanes herself through prostitution is to be burned. Finally, they must keep away from holy things while unclean, eating them only after being clean and bathing, or face sin and death, and they must not cause the people's holy things to bear guilt.

The Tent of Meeting is the sacred place where the LORD speaks to Moses and dwells with the children of Israel, even amid their uncleanness. Its door is the central site for worship: offerers bring burnt offerings and sin-offering bulls there, the altar of burnt offering stands before it, and offerings made elsewhere bring blood guilt and being cut off. Inside, the priest sprinkles blood before the veil and on the altar of sweet incense. The records progress from sacrifice procedures (Leviticus 1, 4), to the congregation's assembly and the seven-day ordination of Aaron and his sons (8), to the Day of Atonement, when Aaron alone enters and leaves his linen garments (16), ending with the rule that all offerings must be brought to its door (17).

The altar of burnt offering stands at the door of the Tent of Meeting. In Leviticus 1 it receives sprinkled blood, fire and wood, and burnt offerings; a flock animal is killed on its north side, and a bird's crop and feathers are cast beside it on the east, where the ashes go. In chapter 3 Aaron's sons sprinkle offering blood on it and burn fat portions there. In chapter 4 sin offering blood is put on its horns or poured at its base, and the fat is burned on it.

The burnt offering is offered to the LORD and makes atonement for the offerer. It may come from the herd, flock, or birds; animals must be unblemished males. The animal is killed, cut up, washed, and wholly burned on the altar, a pleasant aroma to the LORD; a bird is torn by its wings but not divided.

An offerer, a member of the children of Israel, brings a livestock offering to the Tent of Meeting door to be accepted before the LORD, lays a hand on the burnt offering for atonement, then kills, skins, cuts and washes it.

After the sin offering is made, the priest makes atonement for the offender or group. The text states that they "shall be forgiven" or "will be forgiven." This is stated for the congregation, the ruler, the common person, and the one who brings a lamb. Atonement is made by the priest for the guilty person concerning his sin, each time after the required offering. It results in the person being forgiven. It is made with the ram in the cases of trespass against holy things and unwitting sin.
Fire from before the LORD consumes the burnt offering and altar fat, prompting all the people to shout and fall on their faces.

The meal offering is a most holy offering made of fine flour with oil and frankincense, presented to the LORD through Aaron's sons, the priests. It may be baked in an oven, made on a griddle or in a pan, and a first fruits version uses parched, crushed fresh grain. It must contain no yeast or honey and is seasoned with salt. The priest burns a handful of flour, oil and all the frankincense on the altar as a memorial portion for a pleasant aroma. The remainder belongs to Aaron and his sons, shared equally, and every male eats it unleavened in a holy place. The priest's own meal offering, made on a griddle with oil, is wholly burned.
Salt is the covenant salt of God, which must never be lacking; it seasons every meal offering and is to be offered with all offerings, per Chapter 2.

The sacrifice of peace offerings is an offering made by fire with a pleasant aroma to the LORD. Brought from herd or flock, without defect, it involves laying a hand on the head, killing at the Tent of Meeting, sprinkling blood, and burning fat on the altar.

l: offerer (the person bringing the offering), Leviticus
s: lays_hand_on herd animal (offering from the herd) [on its head] The offerer brings an animal without defect before the LORD, lays his hand on its head, and kills it at the Tent of Meeting. He also takes away the specified fat, kidneys, and liver cover as the offering made by fire.

l: herd animal (offering from the herd), Leviticus
s: A male or female herd animal offered as a peace offering, required to be without defect; the offerer lays a hand on its head, it is killed at the Tent of Meeting door, and its fat, kidneys and liver cover are burned on the altar.

A flock lamb, male or female and without defect, offered as a peace offering before the LORD: killed before the Tent of Meeting, then its entire tail fat, removed close to the backbone, is taken and burned as food of the fire offering.

A goat is a peace offering presented before the LORD: a hand is laid on its head, it is killed at the Tent of Meeting, and the priest burns its fat, kidneys and liver cover on the altar as a pleasant aroma.

belongs_to LORD [all the fat] The fat covering the innards, the fat on the kidneys by the loins, the liver cover, and for a lamb the tail fat are taken away and burned on the altar. The text states that all the fat is the LORD's, and the people are forbidden to eat it.
The blood of each peace offering is sprinkled around on the altar by Aaron's sons. The people are forbidden to eat blood as part of a perpetual statute.

l: perpetual statute against eating fat and blood, Leviticus
s: A perpetual statute closing Chapter 3, binding all generations in all dwellings, forbidding the people from eating fat or blood.

offers young bull [sin offering when the sin becomes known] If the whole congregation sins and the matter is hidden from the assembly, then once the sin is known the assembly must offer a young bull as a sin offering. The elders lay their hands on its head, and after the prescribed rites the priest makes atonement and they are forgiven.

The anointed priest is a role whose sin can bring guilt on the people. He must offer a young bull without defect as a sin offering, performing blood rites: sprinkling seven times before the veil, applying blood to the incense altar's horns, and pouring the rest at the burnt offering altar's base. Atonement and forgiveness follow.

offers goat (ruler's offering) [sin offering when his sin is made known to him] When a ruler unwittingly sins and the sin is made known to him, he must bring a male goat without defect as his offering. He lays his hand on it and it is killed, and after the priest's rites he is forgiven.

offers goat (common person's offering) [sin offering when sin is made known] When one of the common people unwittingly sins and it is made known to him, he brings a female goat without defect. He may alternatively bring a female lamb without defect. After the priest makes atonement, he is forgiven.

The sin offering is the prescribed sacrifice for unintentional sins, with the animal varying by the offender's status. The offerer lays a hand on its head, it is killed before the LORD at the place of the burnt offering, its blood is applied to the altar, and its fat is burned. It is most holy: the offering priest and male priests of Aaron's line eat it in a holy place, the court of the Tent of Meeting, and whatever touches its flesh becomes holy. Blood-splashed garments and cooking vessels require washing, scouring, or breaking. If its blood enters the Tent of Meeting for atonement, it is burned, not eaten.

is_a sin against the LORD's commands [done unwittingly, against things the LORD commanded not to be done] The chapter addresses sins done unintentionally or unwittingly, in any of the things the LORD has commanded not to be done. It covers the anointed priest, the whole congregation, a ruler, and the common people. The offering is required when the sin becomes known, and it makes the offender guilty until atonement is made.

required_condition without defect [sin offering for the anointed priest] A young bull without defect is the sin offering for the anointed priest and for the whole congregation. It is killed at the door of the Tent of Meeting before the LORD. Its fat is burned on the altar, and the rest of it (skin, meat, head, legs, innards, dung) is carried outside the camp to a clean place where ashes are poured out and burned on wood.

The ruler's sin offering is a male goat without defect. The ruler lays a hand on its head and kills it before the LORD; the priest applies blood to the altar's horns, pours out the rest at the base, and burns all the fat.

Blood is the central element of the sin offering rites in Chapter 4. For the priest and congregation, it is sprinkled seven times before the veil and put on the incense altar's horns; for a ruler or common person, it goes on the burnt offering altar's horns. In all cases the remainder is poured at that altar's base.

Peace offerings are a category of sacrifice governed by rules that differ by type. A thanksgiving offering comes with unleavened cakes and wafers with oil and must be eaten on the day offered. Vow or freewill offerings may be eaten that day and the next; leftovers on the third day are burned and bring iniquity. Unclean contact requires burning, and eating while unclean means being cut off. Priests receive the breast and right thigh.

The burnt offering is a sacrificial rite: it remains on the altar hearth all night until morning, is laid in order on the altar fire each morning, its skin goes to the offering priest, and the sin offering is killed where it is killed.

The priest is an officiant who makes atonement for guilty persons so they are forgiven. He handles bird sin offerings and altar blood, burns a memorial handful of flour, keeps the remainder as a meal offering, and receives restitution plus a fifth.

A person who sins becomes guilty by failing to testify, unknowingly touching uncleanness, swearing rashly, or trespassing against holy things. He bears iniquity, must confess, bring an offering suited to his means, and make restitution plus a fifth; priestly atonement brings forgiveness.

The sin offering is a sacrifice scaled to the sinner's means: a female lamb or goat; if poor, two turtledoves or young pigeons; if poorer still, a tenth of an ephah of fine flour without oil or frankincense. The bird's blood is sprinkled on the altar's side and drained at its base.

The trespass offering is a most holy offering brought by a guilty person to the LORD, typically a ram without defect from the flock, valued in silver by the sanctuary shekel and brought to the priest. Chapter 5 presents it for sin regarding holy things or unwitting sin, declaring the bringer guilty before the LORD. Chapter 6 adds that the priest makes atonement through it and the offender is forgiven. Chapter 7 gives the procedure: it is killed where the burnt offering is killed, its blood sprinkled around the altar, and its fat, kidneys and liver cover burned by the priest. Male priests eat the rest in a holy place, and the officiating priest owns it, under one law with the sin offering. Chapter 14 shows a different use: a male lamb is waved with oil, followed by sin, burnt and meal offerings, with a poorer person bringing one male lamb plus two doves or pigeons.

is_valued_in shekel of the sanctuary [estimated in silver] A ram without defect from the flock is the required trespass offering for unwitting trespass against the LORD's holy things and for unknowingly breaking his commands. It is valued in silver by the shekel of the sanctuary. The priest makes atonement with it, and the person is forgiven.

l: holy things of the LORD, Leviticus
s: Holy things are offerings the children of Israel consecrate to the LORD, which priests eat as their bread, only while clean. Eating is restricted to the priest's household: purchased slaves, those born in his house, and a widowed or divorced childless daughter returned home. Strangers, foreigners living with priests, hired servants, and a daughter married to an outsider may not eat them; unwitting eating requires adding a fifth and giving the holy thing to the priest.
Restitution obliges a guilty person to return robbed, oppressed, deposited, found, or falsely sworn goods in full, adding a fifth part, and give it to the owner on the day of conviction.

Unwitting sin, trespass against the LORD's holy things or doing forbidden acts unknowingly, still leaves a person guilty. It is atoned by a defect-free ram as trespass offering brought to the priest; holy things also require restitution plus a fifth, then forgiveness follows.

The priest, of Aaron's line, makes atonement for offenders with the trespass offering, resulting in forgiveness. He tends the altar by wearing linen, burning wood each morning, and removing ashes outside the camp in other garments. He eats the sin offering in a holy place, shared by male priests, but his own meal offering is wholly burned.

Trespass against a neighbor is also a sin against the LORD, including false dealing in deposits, bargains, robbery, oppression, and lying about found lost property; it demands full restitution plus a fifth and a trespass offering.

must_make restitution [on being found guilty] The offender who is found guilty must restore what he took, add a fifth part, and return it to its owner on the day he is found guilty. He then brings a ram without defect to the priest as a trespass offering and is forgiven after the priest makes atonement.

The altar is a sacred place of offering. It keeps the burnt offering burning all night, receives the meal offering, and has its ashes set beside it. Moses sanctifies it and its vessels by anointing oil and blood on its horns and base, then burns offerings on it. Aaron later makes offerings there, putting blood on its horns and base, and fire from before the LORD consumes the burnt offering and fat.

burns continuously [must not go out] The fire on the altar must be kept burning continually and must not go out. The priest burns wood on it every morning, lays the burnt offering in order on it, and burns the fat of the peace offerings on it.

Aaron is clothed with the tunic, sash, robe, ephod with its skillfully woven band, breastplate holding the Urim and Thummim, turban, and golden plate, the holy crown. His sons receive tunics, sashes, and headbands, and the garments are sprinkled with oil and blood to sanctify them.

Every male among the priests may eat the trespass offering in a holy place. The priest who makes atonement keeps the sin and trespass offerings, and the priest who offers a burnt offering keeps its skin. The priest who offers a baked, pan or griddle meal offering keeps it, and the priest who sprinkles the blood of the peace offerings receives the heave offering portion. The priest burns the fat on the altar.

l: ordination of Aaron and his sons, Leviticus
s: A LORD-commanded ordination of Aaron and his sons, performed by Moses before the congregation through washing, clothing, anointing, and offerings to make atonement, concluding with a seven-day stay at the Tent of Meeting door, with all commands obeyed.

Fat is a ritual matter: the children of Israel are forbidden to eat the fat of bull, sheep or goat, while priests burn offering fat on the altar. Fat of animals that died or were torn may serve other uses, never eaten; eating offered fat brings being cut off.

is_forbidden_to children of Israel [bird or animal, in any dwelling; penalty is being cut off] The blood of the trespass offering is sprinkled around on the altar. The children of Israel may not eat any blood, of bird or animal, in any dwelling, and whoever eats it is cut off from his people. The priest who sprinkles the blood of the peace offerings receives a portion.

l: peace offerings (waved breast and heaved thigh), Leviticus
s: Peace offering portions: the breast, waved before the LORD, belongs to Aaron and his sons; the right thigh, a heave offering, goes to the priest who offers the blood and fat. The LORD decrees these portions given to Aaron and his sons forever from Israel.

Uncleanness is a ritual state arising from leprosy, discharge, touching the dead, seminal emission, or a creeping thing. It lasts until evening, requires bathing before eating holy things after sundown, and approaching holy things while unclean means being cut off.

assembles_at Tent of Meeting [at the door] The congregation is assembled at the door of the Tent of Meeting at the LORD's command. Moses tells them that this is the thing the LORD has commanded to be done.

Anointing oil is a sanctifying substance Moses uses in Chapter 8: he anoints the tabernacle and its contents, sprinkles the altar and vessels, pours it on Aaron's head, then sprinkles oil mixed with altar blood on Aaron, his sons, and garments.

l: bull of the sin offering, Leviticus
s: A sin offering bull: Aaron and his sons lay hands on its head, it is killed, its blood purifies the altar for atonement, its fat, liver cover and kidneys burn on the altar, and the rest burns outside the camp.

l: ram of the burnt offering, Leviticus
s: is_a burnt offering [pleasant aroma, offering made by fire to the LORD] Aaron and his sons lay their hands on this ram, which is killed, and its blood is sprinkled around the altar. It is cut into pieces, and after the innards and legs are washed, the whole ram is burned on the altar as a pleasant aroma, an offering made by fire to the LORD.

The ram of consecration is a second ram, presented after the burnt offering ram, offered by fire to the LORD as a pleasant aroma. Aaron and his sons lay hands on it; it is killed, its blood applied to their ear, thumb and toe and sprinkled on the altar; fat and thigh burned, breast to Moses, meat eaten.

appears_to children of Israel [to all the people after the blessing] Moses promises that the LORD's glory will appear to the people once they do what was commanded. After Moses and Aaron come out of the Tent of Meeting and bless the people, the LORD's glory appears to all the people.

Sin offering ritual in which Aaron sacrifices a calf for himself, then a goat for the people. Blood goes on the altar's horns, fat, kidneys and liver cover burn on the altar, and meat and skin burn outside the camp; the goat follows likewise.

A burnt offering of unblemished animals: a ram for Aaron, and a calf and year-old lamb for the people. Aaron kills his, sons deliver blood to sprinkle around the altar, pieces, head, innards and legs are burned, the people's offering follows ordinance, then fire from the LORD consumes it.

has_part bull (peace offering) [for the people] A bull and a ram are commanded as the people's peace offerings, and Aaron kills them, with his sons delivering the blood to be sprinkled around the altar. The fat, fat tail, innard covering, kidneys, and liver cover are burned on the altar, and Aaron waves the breasts and right thigh as a wave offering before the LORD.

Nadab, a son of Aaron, took his censer with fire and incense and offered uncommanded strange fire before the LORD; he was devoured by fire from the LORD, died, and his body was carried out of the camp in his tunic.
Abihu, a son of Aaron, offered uncommanded strange fire before the LORD with Nadab, using his censer; he was devoured by fire from the LORD, died, and was carried out of the camp in his tunic.

has_status anointed [anointing oil is on him] Eleazar, a son of Aaron who survives, is told by Moses not to let his hair go loose or tear his clothes and not to leave the Tent of Meeting. He is told to eat the remaining meal offering beside the altar, and Moses is angry with him and Ithamar when the sin offering goat is found burned.

has_status anointed [anointing oil is on him] Ithamar, a son of Aaron who survives, is told by Moses not to let his hair go loose or tear his clothes and not to leave the Tent of Meeting. He is told to eat the remaining meal offering beside the altar, and Moses is angry with him and Eleazar when the sin offering goat is found burned.

l: strange fire (offered by Nadab and Abihu), Leviticus
s: has_status not commanded by the LORD The strange fire was placed in censers with incense and offered before the LORD by Nadab and Abihu. The text says the LORD had not commanded it, and it precedes their death.
Fire from before the LORD, a burning the LORD kindled, comes out and devours Nadab and Abihu, who die; Moses says Israel may mourn.

l: wine and strong drink prohibition, Leviticus
s: A divine command forbids Aaron and his sons wine or strong drink when entering the Tent of Meeting, on penalty of death, as a perpetual statute across generations, tied to distinguishing holy from common and teaching Israel.

l: offerings and bread of God, Leviticus
s: has_status most holy The priests offer the LORD's offerings made by fire, called the bread of their God, which is the reason they must be holy. Only priests without defects may draw near to offer it, though a defective priest may eat of both the most holy and the holy portions.
A most holy sin offering goat, meant to bear the congregation's iniquity for atonement; Moses found it burned rather than eaten in the sanctuary, became angry, but was pleased by Aaron's explanation.

l: death of Nadab and Abihu, Leviticus
s: Nadab and Abihu are devoured by fire from the LORD for offering strange fire; Mishael and Elzaphan carry their bodies out of camp, while Aaron, Eleazar, Ithamar may not mourn.

purpose distinguish unclean from clean and edible from inedible The chapter sets out the distinction between clean animals that may be eaten and unclean ones that may not. It concludes that the law exists to make a distinction between the unclean and the clean, and between the living thing that may be eaten and the one that may not.

Chapter 11's dietary rules for land animals: only those with a parted, cloven hoof that chew the cud may be eaten. The camel, hyrax, hare and pig each meet only one test, so they are unclean, untouchable carcasses, as are paw-walkers. Israel must distinguish clean from unclean.
Water creatures are classified by body features: those with fins and scales may be eaten, while all others lacking them are an abomination, forbidden as food and their carcasses detested.
Chapter 11 declares a list of birds, including eagle, vulture, ravens, owls, heron and hoopoe, an abomination not to be eaten; the bat is added at the end.

Flying insects: winged creeping things walking on all fours are an abomination, but an exception allows those with long jointed hopping legs, so locusts, katydids, crickets, and grasshoppers may be eaten.

Creeping things are a category of animals declared an abomination and not to be eaten. Named unclean examples include weasel, rat, lizards, gecko, skink and chameleon; touching them dead causes uncleanness until evening.

Carcasses are a source of ritual uncleanness: touching or carrying one, even of an edible animal that died, makes a person unclean until evening, with clothes washed for carriers. Items they fall on become unclean, requiring washing or breaking, except springs, cisterns, and dry seed.

Rules on uncleanness and purification: touching or carrying carcasses brings uncleanness until evening, with clothes washed. Vessels go into water and are clean by evening; earthen vessels and ovens are broken. Soaked food or drink becomes unclean, while springs, cisterns and dry sowing seed are exceptions.

Holiness is a state the LORD commands of Israel, required of the children of Israel because He is holy. In Chapter 11 it is pursued by avoiding defilement from creeping things and keeping clean/unclean distinctions; Chapter 20 repeats the command, adding that He set them apart as His, to keep His statutes.

l: woman who bears a child, Leviticus
s: A woman who bears a child is ritually unclean afterward. Uncleanness lasts seven days for a male child and two weeks for a female, followed by blood of purification for thirty-three or sixty-six days respectively. Throughout, she may not touch holy things or enter the sanctuary. When the days are completed, she brings a year-old lamb for a burnt offering and a pigeon or turtledove for a sin offering to the priest, who makes atonement. If poor, she brings two turtledoves or pigeons.

l: male child (born to the woman), Leviticus
s: undergoes circumcision [on the eighth day] The male child is circumcised on the eighth day. His birth makes his mother unclean for seven days, followed by thirty-three days in the blood of purification.

l: female child (born to the woman), Leviticus
s: The birth of a female child makes her mother unclean for two weeks, followed by sixty-six days in the blood of purification. The same offerings are required as for a son.
A priest who receives a postpartum woman's offerings at the Tent of Meeting door, offers them before the LORD, and makes atonement for her, after which she is clean, including with two birds.

is_like monthly period [uncleanness as in the days of her period] A woman who bears a son is unclean seven days, as in her monthly period, and one who bears a daughter is unclean two weeks. The uncleanness is followed by a further period in the blood of purification during which she may not touch holy things or enter the sanctuary.

results_in cleansing from the fountain of her blood [after the priest makes atonement] The blood of purification lasts thirty-three days after a son and sixty-six days after a daughter. When these days are completed, the woman brings her offerings, and the priest's atonement cleanses her from the fountain of her blood.

is_made_with lamb [a year old] A year old lamb is to be brought as a burnt offering when the days of purification are completed. If the woman cannot afford a lamb, one of two turtledoves or young pigeons serves as the burnt offering.

is_made_with pigeons and turtledoves [young pigeon or turtledove] A young pigeon or a turtledove is brought as the sin offering when the days of purification are completed. If the woman cannot afford a lamb, the second of her two birds is the sin offering.
A year old lamb is the prescribed burnt offering for the woman after her purification days. If she cannot afford one, two turtledoves or two young pigeons are allowed in its place.

A young pigeon or a turtledove is the sin offering the woman brings with her lamb. If she cannot afford a lamb, she takes two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one for the burnt offering and the other for the sin offering.

The priest is the examiner of leprosy plagues, judging depth, hair color, and spread. He isolates uncertain cases for seven days at a time, then pronounces persons or garments clean or unclean, commanding washing or burning of affected garments.

Leprosy is described through signs such as a swelling, scab, or bright spot deeper than the skin, white hair in the plague, and raw flesh. It can break out in a boil, a burn, or on the head or beard, and a dull white rash is not leprosy. If it covers all the flesh and has turned white, the person is clean, but raw flesh makes them unclean.

The infected person, a leper, is examined by a priest, possibly isolated for seven days or more, and pronounced clean or unclean. If declared leprous, he wears torn clothes, lets his hair hang loose, covers his upper lip, cries 'Unclean! Unclean!', and dwells alone outside the camp while the plague lasts. Once healed, he is sprinkled seven times, washes, shaves, and bathes, then stays outside his tent seven days. On the eighth day he brings lambs to the Tent of Meeting, receives blood and oil, and is made clean by atonement.

Mildew is a greenish or reddish destructive plague affecting wool, linen, or leather, treated like leprosy; after washing, spreading or unchanged color means unclean and burning, while fading means tearing out the affected part.

is_burned_when mildew spreads [destructive mildew] A garment of wool, linen, or leather with a greenish or reddish plague is shown to the priest and isolated for seven days. If the plague spreads it is burned, but if it does not spread it is washed and isolated seven more days. If the plague departs after washing, the garment is washed a second time and is clean.

The priest is an officiant who judges and restores cleanness. In Chapter 14 he goes outside the camp to examine a leper, directs the two-bird ritual, sprinkles, and pronounces the person clean. On the eighth day he offers sacrifices, applies blood and oil, and makes atonement. He also inspects a mildewed house, orders it emptied, and pronounces it clean or demolished.

Leprosy is a plague making a person unclean until a priest examines and finds him healed. A two-bird cleansing ritual marks the day of cleansing. The law, grouped with itch, mildew, swelling, scab, and bright spot, teaches distinguishing clean from unclean.

l: cleansing ritual for the leper (two birds), Leviticus
s: A ritual for cleansing a leper: the priest has two living clean birds, cedar wood, scarlet, and hyssop brought. One bird is killed over running water in an earthen vessel; the living bird and materials are dipped in its blood. The person is sprinkled seven times and pronounced clean, the living bird is released into the open field, and the same ritual cleanses a mildewed house.

The land of Canaan is the place the LORD is bringing Israel to, and it was defiled by the abominations of the nations before them. The LORD punished its iniquity and the land vomited out its inhabitants, and it is warned it will do the same to Israel if they defile it.

A house in Canaan afflicted with spreading mildew, shown by greenish or reddish hollow streaks. The owner reports it to the priest, who has it emptied and shut up seven days. If the plague spreads, stones are removed and the house scraped and replastered. If mildew returns, it is destructive, unclean and broken down, its materials taken outside the city; if not, it is pronounced clean and cleansed with the bird ritual.

A man with a discharge is ceremonially unclean whether it runs or has stopped, and he spreads uncleanness to his bed, seat, saddle, and vessels he touches; earthen vessels are broken. Anyone touching him or these must wash and is unclean until evening. After cleansing he counts seven days, bathes in running water, and on the eighth day brings two birds to the priest for atonement.

A woman with a bloody discharge is impure seven days, making her bedding, seats, and anyone touching them unclean. If discharge outlasts her period, she stays unclean throughout. After cleansing she waits seven days, then on the eighth brings two birds, a sin and burnt offering, so the priest atones for her.
A priest who, on the eighth day at the Tent of Meeting door, receives two birds from a man or woman with a discharge, offers one as sin offering and one as burnt offering, and atones before the LORD.

endangers children of Israel [they could die in their uncleanness defiling the tabernacle] Uncleanness is created by discharges and by emission of semen, and it spreads through touch, lying, or sitting to people and objects. It usually lasts until evening, but longer in some cases, such as seven days for a man who lies with a menstruating woman, and it can defile the tabernacle and bring death.

A bodily discharge, whether flowing or stopped, makes a man unclean, and a woman's blood discharge outside her period makes her unclean for its duration. Cleansing requires seven days of counting, washing, and bathing, followed by offerings on the eighth day.

Emission of semen is a cause of ritual uncleanness: the man must bathe his whole body and stays unclean until evening; affected garments and skin are washed, and a couple lying together with an emission both bathe and share the same uncleanness.

A woman's period brings seven days of impurity: her bed and seat become unclean, touching her or them makes one unclean until evening, a man lying with her is unclean seven days, and extra discharge counts like her period.

required_after touching unclean things [wash clothes, bathe, unclean until evening] Washing clothes and bathing in water are required of those who touch an unclean person or object, and they stay unclean until evening. A person cleansed of a discharge must bathe in running water after the seven days, and garments with semen on them are washed.

l: sin offering and burnt offering, Leviticus
s: On the eighth day after cleansing, a man or woman with a discharge brings two turtledoves or young pigeons to the priest, one for a sin offering and one for a burnt offering. The priest offers them to make atonement before the LORD for the discharge.

The Most Holy Place lies within the veil, containing the mercy seat on the ark where the LORD appears in the cloud; Aaron may enter only at the prescribed time and manner, with incense and sprinkled blood, or die.

l: bull of the sin offering (Aaron's bull), Leviticus
s: is_offered_for Aaron [for himself and his house] The young bull is the sin offering for Aaron himself and his house, and he kills it. Its blood is sprinkled on the mercy seat and seven times before it, and some is put on the altar's horns. Its skin, flesh, and dung are burned outside the camp.

l: goat for the LORD (sin offering goat), Leviticus
s: The goat chosen by lot for the LORD is offered as a sin offering for the people; Aaron kills it, brings its blood within the veil as with the bull's blood, and it is later burned outside the camp.

The scapegoat is a goat chosen by lot and presented alive before the LORD for atonement. Aaron confesses Israel's iniquities over its head, it carries them to a solitary land and is released in the wilderness; its releaser must wash and bathe.

The day of atonement falls on the tenth day of the seventh month and is a holy convocation, a Sabbath of solemn rest, and a statute forever, kept from evening to evening. Its purpose is to make atonement before the LORD, cleansing the children of Israel from all their sins. The people, native-born and stranger alike, must afflict their souls, do no work, and offer an offering made by fire. Whoever does not deny himself is cut off from his people, and whoever works is destroyed by the LORD. Chapter 16 sets the day and its cleansing; Chapter 23 adds the penalties.

Atonement is made by Aaron for himself and his house, for the Holy Place, the Tent of Meeting, the altar, the priests, and all the people. It is accomplished through blood sprinkling, incense, and the sending away of the live goat, and it is to be done once a year as an everlasting statute, cleansing Israel from all their sins.

Foreigners living among the children of Israel are bound by the same rules as Israelites: bringing offerings to the Tent of Meeting and avoiding blood, with cleansing and uncleanness until evening required if they eat carcasses.
A priest who receives peace offering sacrifices brought to the Tent of Meeting door, sprinkles their blood on the LORD's altar, then burns the fat as a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
The LORD's altar at the Tent of Meeting's door, where the priest sprinkles sacrificial blood, which the LORD gave to make atonement for souls.

Blood is presented as the life of the flesh, given by the LORD on the altar to make atonement. Eating it is forbidden to Israelites and resident strangers, on penalty of being cut off. Hunted animals' blood must be poured out and covered with dust; killing without the Tent of Meeting counts as shed blood.

Sacrifices are a regulation: they must be brought to the Tent of Meeting door and offered to the LORD as peace offerings through the priest, never in open fields or to goat idols; violators are cut off, a permanent statute.
The LORD says he gave the blood on the altar to make atonement for the people's souls. It is the blood, by reason of the life in it, that makes atonement.

Molech is the recipient of offspring given by anyone among the children of Israel or the strangers living in Israel. Those who play the prostitute after Molech are to be put to death or cut off from their people.

l: nations (those cast out of the land), Leviticus
s: The nations the LORD is casting out before Israel defiled themselves with these abominations, and the land became defiled. Because of this the LORD punished the land's iniquity and the land vomited out its inhabitants, serving as a warning to Israel.

This topic covers forbidden sexual relations, described as uncovering nakedness. Chapter 18 lists prohibited unions with close relatives, a woman and her daughter, a sister's co-wife, a woman during impurity, a neighbor's wife, a male, and an animal, calling them abomination, defilement, wickedness, and perversion, with offenders cut off from their people. Chapter 20 repeats a long list with stated penalties: death, burning, being cut off, or dying childless.

must_be kept [by Israel] The LORD commands Israel to do his ordinances and keep his statutes and walk in them, in contrast to the statutes of Egypt and Canaan. A man who does them 'shall live in them.' Keeping them means avoiding the listed abominations and keeping the LORD's requirements.

Child sacrifice to Molech is forbidden by the LORD. Offenders are punished by death through stoning by the people of the land, because it defiles his sanctuary and profanes his holy name. If people ignore it, he will cut off the offender, his family, and followers.

requires observance of all statutes and ordinances The chapter sets out the commandments that express holiness: respecting parents, keeping Sabbaths, avoiding idols, honest dealing, justice without partiality, and loving one's neighbor. It also includes rules on offerings, harvest, fruit trees, blood, sorcery, mediums, bodily practices, and just weights and measures, all ending with a call to observe every statute and ordinance.

The Sabbath is the LORD's solemn rest and holy convocation on the seventh day, kept in all dwellings after six days of work. In Chapter 23 it is established first, serves as a dating reference for the wave sheaf and counting seven Sabbaths, and names the day of atonement. In Chapter 26 it is commanded, and the desolate land receives its missed Sabbaths.

A non-priestly outsider living as a foreigner in the land, who must not be wronged but treated as native-born and loved as oneself, since Israel was once foreign in Egypt; field and vineyard gleanings are left for him.
A neighbor is someone protected from oppression, robbery, and endangerment; Chapter 19 forbids harming or hating neighbors, requiring righteous judgment, rebuke, and love as oneself.

is_punished_by death [stoning] Anyone who turns to mediums and wizards is described as playing the prostitute after them, and the LORD will set his face against that person and cut him off from his people. A man or woman who is a medium or wizard is to be put to death by stoning, with their blood upon themselves.

The land responds to Israel's conduct: obedience brings increase, fruit, and safety; disobedience makes it iron-hard, unproductive, then desolate, its cities waste. During exile it rests and enjoys its Sabbaths, and the LORD remembers it.

executes stoning [for those who give offspring to Molech] The people of the land are commanded to stone anyone who gives offspring to Molech. The LORD warns that if they all hide their eyes and do not put the offender to death, he will set his face against the man and his family and cut them off.
is_punished_by death [both adulterer and adulteress] Adultery with another man's wife, or a neighbor's wife, is punished by the death of both the adulterer and the adulteress.

is_abhorred_by the LORD [because of its practices] The LORD is casting this nation out before Israel because they did all the forbidden things, and he abhorred them. Israel is told not to walk in its customs.

The land is described as flowing with milk and honey and is given by the LORD to the children of Israel to inherit and possess, though it remains the LORD's own, with Israelites as strangers and foreigners. Chapter 20 warns it may vomit them out if they ignore his statutes and ordinances. Chapter 25 says it keeps a Sabbath, cannot be sold in perpetuity, and brings abundance and safety, with rules for houses and Levite pasture lands.

The high priest is a consecrated figure whose head is anointed with oil and who wears the sacred garments. He is bound by strict restrictions: no loose hair, torn clothes, contact with dead bodies (even parents), or leaving the sanctuary. He must marry only a virgin of his own people to avoid profaning offspring.

l: mourning and contact with the dead, Leviticus
s: permitted_for_priests_only_for near relatives [mother, father, son, daughter, brother, virgin sister] A priest may not defile himself for the dead among his people, except for his mother, father, son, daughter, brother, and his unmarried virgin sister who is near to him. The high priest is forbidden even this and may not defile himself for his father or mother. Priests also may not shave their heads, shave the corners of their beards, or cut their flesh.

Marriage restrictions for priests in Chapter 21: an ordinary priest may not wed a prostitute, profane woman, or divorced woman because he is holy to God; the high priest faces stricter rules, must marry a virgin of his own people, avoiding profaning his offspring.

Physical defects disqualify Aaron's descendants from priestly service. Chapter 21 lists them: blindness, lameness, flat nose, deformity, injured foot or hand, hunchback, dwarfism, eye defect, itching disease, scabs, damaged testicles. Such a man may not offer the offerings or bread of God, nor approach the veil or altar, lest sanctuaries be profaned, but may still eat most holy and holy food.

Offerings are sacrifices presented so the giver is accepted. Burnt offerings must be unblemished males, burned on the altar, and foreigners in Israel may offer vows or free will gifts. Animals qualify from the eighth day, a cow or ewe and its young are not killed together, and thanksgiving sacrifices are eaten the same day.

excludes blind, injured, maimed, warty, festering or running-sore animals [unacceptable for offering] Offerings of bulls, sheep, or goats must be males without defect to be accepted. Animals that are blind, injured, maimed, warty, festering, running with sores, or with bruised, crushed, broken, or cut testicles may not be offered. An animal with a deformity may be given as a free will offering but not accepted for a vow, and defective animals from a foreigner's hand are also not accepted.

l: set feasts of the LORD, Leviticus
s: The LORD's set feasts are his own appointed times, proclaimed as holy convocations in season. They run in order: Sabbath, Passover, unleavened bread, first fruits and fifty-day feast, trumpets, atonement, booths, each with its offerings beyond Sabbaths, gifts, vows, free will offerings.
occurs_on fourteenth day of first month, in the evening The LORD's Passover is set on the fourteenth day of the first month, in the evening.

The feast of unleavened bread begins on the fifteenth day of the first month and lasts seven days, with unleavened bread eaten throughout. The first and seventh days are holy convocations without regular work, and fire offerings go to the LORD daily.

l: offering of the first fruits sheaf, Leviticus
s: The offering of the first fruits sheaf is a ritual commanded for after the people enter the land and reap its harvest. They bring a sheaf to the priest, who waves it before the LORD on the day after the Sabbath. That day a year-old unblemished male lamb is burnt, with a fine flour and oil meal offering and a wine drink offering. Until it is brought, no new grain may be eaten, a statute forever.

l: feast of weeks (Pentecost, fifty days after the sheaf), Leviticus
s: The feast of weeks is a holy convocation, a statute forever with no regular work. It is dated by counting seven completed Sabbaths from the wave sheaf, then fifty days to a new meal offering. The people bring two yeast-baked loaves of fine flour as a first-fruits wave offering, along with burnt offerings of seven lambs, a young bull and two rams, a goat sin offering, and two lambs as peace offerings.

l: day of trumpets (first day of seventh month), Leviticus
s: is_a solemn rest and memorial of trumpet blowing [holy convocation] The first day of the seventh month is a solemn rest and a memorial of blowing of trumpets, a holy convocation. No regular work is to be done, and an offering made by fire is brought to the LORD.

The feast of booths is a perpetual statute kept in the seventh month. It begins on the fifteenth day with a holy convocation and lasts seven days, during which people gather fruit of majestic trees, palm branches, boughs and willows, rejoice before the LORD, and native-born Israelites dwell in temporary shelters, commemorating Israel's shelters after leaving Egypt. A solemn assembly closes it on the eighth day.

is_in_addition_to Sabbaths, gifts, vows, free will offerings [feast offerings each on its own day] The feasts call for offerings made by fire, including burnt offerings, meal offerings, sacrifices, and drink offerings, each on its own day. The unit specifies animals and flour amounts for the first fruits and the fifty-day feast. It states that these are in addition to the Sabbaths, gifts, vows, and free will offerings given to the LORD.

l: son of the Israelite woman, Leviticus
s: Son of Shelomith of Dan and an Egyptian father, he fights a man of Israel in the camp, blasphemes and curses the Name, is held in custody, then stoned outside the camp.

has_penalty death by stoning [applies to foreigner and native-born alike] The son of the Israelite woman blasphemes the Name and curses during a quarrel. The LORD declares that whoever blasphemes his name shall surely be put to death by stoning by all the congregation, foreigner and native-born alike.

is_carried_out_by children of Israel [outside the camp, as the LORD commanded Moses] The LORD orders that the one who cursed be brought out of the camp, that those who heard him lay their hands on his head, and that all the congregation stone him. The children of Israel do so, as the LORD commanded Moses.

The law of retribution, stated by the LORD in Chapter 24, requires life for life for killing a man and restitution for killing an animal, and prescribes fracture for fracture, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, applying equally to foreigner and native-born.

The Sabbath year is a seventh-year solemn rest for the land: no sowing or pruning, and no reaping of what grows by itself. Its produce feeds people, servants, strangers and livestock, and the LORD promises the sixth year's blessing will supply the seventh.

The Year of Jubilee is a holy observance in the fiftieth year, after seven Sabbaths of years. A trumpet on the Day of Atonement opens it, proclaiming liberty. Each person returns to property and family, and sowing and reaping are forbidden. Land prices and dedicated-field valuations are reduced by years remaining until it. Sold land and indentured Israelites are released, and a dedicated field returns to its original owner or passes to the priests.

A poor brother is an impoverished fellow Israelite protected by law in Chapter 25. He may have sold possessions, which his nearest kinsman or he himself, if prosperous, can redeem. He is upheld like a temporary resident, spared interest and profit, and serves as a hired servant, not a slave. He and his children go free at Jubilee; if sold to a foreigner, redemption is priced by remaining years.

Land redemption is a law requiring redemption rights across all possessed land. A kinsman may buy back sold property, or the seller repays the surplus calculated from years since sale; otherwise release comes at the Jubilee. Walled-city houses allow one year; Levites' houses, anytime.

is_with ancestors [brought out of Egypt; the LORD remembers it for their sake] The LORD promises to establish his covenant with the obedient, while those who reject his statutes and break the covenant face vengeance of the covenant through the sword. Even in exile, the LORD will remember his covenant with Jacob, Isaac, and Abraham and the covenant with their ancestors whom he brought out of Egypt. He will not break it by destroying them utterly.

fall_before Israelites [when Israelites obey] In the blessings, the Israelites chase their enemies, who fall before them by the sword. In the curses, enemies eat the people's seed, rule over them, receive them into their hands, and dwell in the desolated land. The scattered survivors live in the enemies' lands, where they flee in terror and perish.

Blessings promised for obedience, conditioned on walking in statutes and keeping commandments: seasonal rain, abundant harvests, peaceful land without fear or sword, evil animals removed, victory over enemies, then fruitfulness, multiplication, a confirmed covenant, and the LORD dwelling and walking among them.

Chapter 26 describes punishments for Israelite disobedience, rejecting statutes and breaking covenant, in escalating sevenfold stages: terror, consumption, fever, enemy rule, drought, wild animals, sword, pestilence, famine, and cannibalism. They culminate in ruined cities and sanctuaries, scattering among nations, and fainthearted exile, yet remain non-final: confession and humility lead the LORD to remember his covenant.

The priest is an official who assesses values for vows, dedicated animals, unclean animals, houses, and fields; his evaluation stands, adjusts field value by years remaining to the Jubilee, and unredeemed fields become priestly property.

l: vow of consecrating persons and valuation, Leviticus
s: Vow of consecrating persons sets sanctuary-shekel silver values by age and sex. Males aged twenty to sixty are fifty shekels, females thirty; younger and older people are valued lower, down to five and three for infants. Those too poor to pay are set before the priest, who assigns a value by ability.

l: animals dedicated to the LORD, Leviticus
s: Rules for animals dedicated to the LORD: offered animals become holy and cannot be altered or exchanged, since both original and substitute become holy. Unclean animals are priest-valued and redeemable with a fifth added; firstborn animals cannot be dedicated, already belonging to the LORD.
A dedicated house is valued by the priest, and that valuation stands; if the owner redeems it, he adds a fifth of the valuation and keeps it.

A dedicated field is a possessed field consecrated to the LORD, valued by seed at fifty shekels of silver per homer of barley sowing, with the value reduced by years remaining after the Jubilee. If unredeemed or sold, it passes to the priests at the Jubilee; a bought field returns to its original seller.

requires_adding fifth part of the valuation [when redeeming a dedicated unclean animal] Redeeming an unclean animal, a house, a field, or part of the tithe requires paying the valuation plus a fifth part. Redeeming is not allowed for permanently devoted things, and a field that is not redeemed or has been sold cannot be redeemed anymore.

Devoted things are what is permanently given to the LORD, whether man, animal, or field; they are most holy, cannot be sold or redeemed, and a person devoted to destruction cannot be ransomed but is put to death.

The tithe is holy and belongs to the LORD, covering the land's seed and fruit plus every tenth animal passing under the rod. Redeeming produce requires adding a fifth, while the animal tithe allows no examining or exchange and cannot be redeemed.

This document is the biblical Book of Ruth, a four-chapter narrative set in the days of the judges, centered on Naomi, her Moabite daughter-in-law Ruth, and Boaz, a wealthy relative of Naomi's late husband Elimelech. During a famine Elimelech takes his wife Naomi and sons Mahlon and Chilion from Bethlehem to Moab. There Elimelech dies, the sons marry Orpah and Ruth, and after about ten years both sons die. Naomi decides to return to Judah; Orpah turns back, but Ruth clings to her and vows that Naomi's people and God will be hers. In Bethlehem at the start of barley harvest, Naomi asks to be called Mara, reflecting her bitterness. Ruth gleans in the field of Boaz, who praises her loyalty, protects her, feeds her, and has extra grain left for her. Naomi blesses him and names him a near kinsman. Following Naomi's instructions, Ruth goes to the threshing floor at night and asks Boaz to spread his garment over her. Boaz blesses her, calls her a worthy woman, and says a nearer kinsman exists, but promises to act himself if that man will not. He sends her home before dawn with six measures of barley. At the city gate, before ten elders, Boaz offers the nearer kinsman Elimelech's land together with Ruth. The man first agrees, then declines for fear of harming his own inheritance, and confirms it by removing his sandal. Boaz declares he has bought all that belonged to Elimelech, Chilion, and Mahlon, and has purchased Ruth as his wife. The people bless him. Ruth bears a son, the women praise the LORD with Naomi, who nurses the child, and he is named Obed, father of Jesse and grandfather of David. The text closes with the generations from Perez to David.

Naomi is a woman who worships the LORD, wife of Elimelech and mother of Mahlon and Chilion. She went to Moab, where her husband and both sons died, leaving her a widow. She returned to Bethlehem, asking to be called Mara, saying she left full and came home empty. Her daughter-in-law Ruth gleans for them, and Naomi recognizes Boaz as a near kinsman. She guides Ruth to approach him at the threshing floor, then tells her to wait while he settles the matter. Boaz buys Elimelech's field from her. When Ruth's son is born, Naomi takes him to her bosom as nurse, and the neighbor women say a son is born to Naomi, turning her bereavement into restoration.

Ruth is a Moabite woman, first the wife of Mahlon and daughter-in-law of Naomi, who becomes known for extraordinary loyalty. After her husband's death she vows to stay with Naomi until death, adopting Naomi's people and God, and leaves her parents and homeland to return with her to Bethlehem at the start of barley harvest. A foreigner in Israel, she takes refuge under the LORD's wings. She gleans in Boaz's field, calling herself his servant, stays close to his maidens through barley and wheat harvests, and lives with Naomi. Boaz blesses her, and the city knows her as a worthy woman who does not pursue young men, poor or rich. At Naomi's direction she goes to the threshing floor and asks Boaz, a near kinsman, to spread his garment over her. He purchases her along with the field to raise up the dead man's name and takes her as wife. The LORD enables her to conceive, and she bears Obed. The women say she loves Naomi and is better than seven sons.
Orpah is a Moabite woman, daughter-in-law of Naomi through marriage to one of her sons; after weeping and kissing Naomi, she returns to her people and god while Ruth stays.

The LORD, titled Almighty and God of Israel, provides bread to his people, prompting Naomi's return. Naomi invokes his kindness for her daughters-in-law, blames his hand for her losses, and Ruth swears by him.

has_inhabitant Women of Moab Moab is the country where Naomi's family went to live during the famine, and where Elimelech, Mahlon and Chilion died. Orpah and Ruth were Moabite women who married the sons there. Naomi left it after hearing that the LORD had given bread to his people.

is_part_of Judah [Bethlehem Judah] Bethlehem Judah is the home of Elimelech's family, who left it during a famine. When Naomi and Ruth arrived at the beginning of barley harvest, the whole city was excited and asked whether this was Naomi.

Boaz is a mighty man of wealth from Bethlehem, a relative of Naomi's husband and of the family of Elimelech, and a near kinsman of Naomi and Ruth. He owns a field and barley, and employs reapers, a servant over them, and maidens. In Chapter 2 he protects Ruth the Moabitess, commanding his young men not to touch her, welcoming her to stay in his field, praising her kindness to Naomi, and ordering extra grain left for her to glean. In Chapter 3 he is winnowing barley at night, wakes startled at midnight to find Ruth, blesses her as a worthy woman, and says a nearer kinsman exists. He swears to perform the kinsman's duty if the other will not, asks for secrecy, and gives her six measures of barley. In Chapter 4 he meets the nearer kinsman and ten elders at the gate. When the kinsman refuses to redeem Elimelech's land, Boaz takes the right of redemption, buys all that was Elimelech's, Chilion's and Mahlon's, and acquires Ruth as his wife. He marries her and is named in the genealogy as son of Salmon, descendant of Perez, and father of Obed.

l: reapers (Boaz's reapers), The Book of Ruth
s: The reapers answer Boaz's greeting by blessing him in return, and the servant set over them reports that Ruth has gleaned since morning, resting only briefly. At mealtime they pass Ruth parched grain as she sits beside them. Boaz's young men are commanded not to touch, reproach, or rebuke her, and to pull out some grain from the bundles for her.

l: field (Boaz's field), The Book of Ruth
s: Ruth happens to come to the portion of the field belonging to Boaz, who is of Elimelech's family. Boaz tells her to glean only there and stay close to his maidens, and it is the place where she works until evening. She remains in his field through the end of the barley and wheat harvests.

l: gleaning (Ruth's gleaning), The Book of Ruth
s: Ruth's gleaning is an event in Boaz's field: she begins after the reapers seeking favor, Boaz extends it to the sheaves with extra grain pulled out, she gleans until evening, beats out about an ephah of barley, and continues through barley and wheat harvests.

l: near kinsman (of Boaz and Elimelech's family), The Book of Ruth
s: A kinsman nearer to Ruth than Boaz, holding first claim to perform the kinsman's duty. Boaz reveals him in Chapter 3 and offers him the chance first. In Chapter 4 at the gate he agrees to redeem the land, but balks on learning he must also buy it from Ruth, fearing for his inheritance. He cedes the right to Boaz, removing his sandal.

l: threshing floor, The Book of Ruth
s: The threshing floor is where Boaz winnows barley on the night in question. He lies down at the end of the heap of grain there, and Ruth comes softly and lies at his feet. Boaz asks that it not be known that a woman came to the threshing floor, and Ruth leaves there before dawn.

l: kinsman's duty, The Book of Ruth
s: Ruth appeals to Boaz as a near kinsman, and he affirms that he is one but that a nearer kinsman has the first claim. Boaz says that if the nearer kinsman performs the duty, good, but if he will not, Boaz will do it, swearing by the LORD's life. Naomi expects Boaz to settle the matter that same day.
Obed is the son of Boaz and Ruth, named by Naomi's neighbor women, who declare him restorer of life and sustainer of Naomi's old age; nursed by Naomi, he fathers Jesse, grandfather of David.

l: parcel of land (Elimelech's field), The Book of Ruth
s: The parcel that was Elimelech's is being sold by Naomi, and Boaz offers it first to the nearer kinsman before the elders. The kinsman declines to redeem it, and Boaz buys it, along with all that was Elimelech's, Chilion's and Mahlon's.

l: redemption of the land and Ruth, The Book of Ruth
s: purpose raise up the name of the dead [on his inheritance] Boaz offers the redemption first to the near kinsman, who agrees to the land but backs out once he learns it includes buying Ruth to raise up the name of the dead on his inheritance.
