The transfer is formalized by the sandal custom, and Boaz declares before the elders and people that he has bought the land and purchased Ruth so the dead man's name will not be cut off. The people answer "We are witnesses" and bless the arrangement.

1 Chronicles 1-29 is a Hebrew-scripture history that opens with long genealogies and then centers on King David's reign and his preparations for the temple. Chapters 1-9 trace the human line from Adam through Noah's sons, Abraham, Isaac and Israel, then the twelve tribes. Judah and David's descendants (including the royal line to the exile) receive special attention, along with Simeon, Reuben, Gad, Manasseh, Levi (priests, singers, cities), Issachar, Benjamin, Ephraim and Asher. Reuben's birthright passes to Joseph's sons, and the eastern tribes are exiled by Assyria for trespass. Chapter 9 lists those resettled in Jerusalem after Babylon, including priests, Levites and gatekeepers. Chapter 10 turns to narrative: Saul and his sons die at Gilboa against the Philistines, and the LORD gives the kingdom to David. In chapters 11-12 all Israel anoints David at Hebron, he takes Jerusalem's Zion stronghold with Joab as chief, and his mighty men and the tribal warriors who came to make him king are listed. Chapters 13-16 describe the ark: Uzza dies when it is moved on a cart, it rests with Obed-Edom, and David then brings it to Jerusalem carried properly by Levites with music, sacrifices and a thanksgiving psalm, while Michal despises him. Chapter 14 records Hiram's help and victories over the Philistines. In chapter 17 Nathan relays God's refusal to let David build a house; instead God promises David a house and an enduring throne through an offspring who will build the temple. Chapters 18-20 recount David's wars against Philistines, Moab, Zobah, Syria, Edom and Ammon, with Joab and Abishai prominent. Chapter 21 describes David's census prompted by Satan, the pestilence that kills seventy thousand, and his purchase of Ornan's threshing floor, where he builds an altar. Chapters 22-29 show David preparing for Solomon: he stockpiles materials, explains that bloodshed barred him from building, and charges Solomon. He organizes Levites, priestly divisions, singers, gatekeepers, treasurers, army divisions and officials. He gives Solomon the temple plans, and he and the leaders donate lavishly. The book closes with David's prayer, Solomon's second anointing as king, and David's death after forty years of reign.
Adam is named first in the genealogy, heading the line that runs through Seth and Enosh down to Noah.
Noah is a man in Adam's line, father of Shem, Ham, and Japheth, from whom the later descendant lists are traced.
Shem is a father of sons Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Aram and others; the line through Arpachshad runs down to Terah and Abram, called Abraham.
Ham is a father of four sons, Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan, whose descendants are listed in 1 Chronicles 1, including Cush's son Nimrod, a mighty one, and Canaan's firstborn Sidon.
Japheth is a man whose seven sons, including Gomer, Magog, Javan, Tubal and Tiras, are listed in 1 Chronicles 1, with Gomer's and Javan's sons also named.

The Philistines are a recurring enemy of Israel across these records. They first defeat Saul at Mount Gilboa, killing his sons Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua, and take his head and armor, placing the armor in the house of their gods and the head in the house of Dagon. They then occupy cities the Israelites abandon. Later they battle at Pasdammim, camp in the valley of Rephaim, and hold a garrison in Bethlehem. When David is anointed king over all Israel, they pursue him but are beaten at Baal Perazim, leaving their gods to be burned, and are struck from Gibeon to Gezer. David subdues them and takes Gath, and some of the silver and gold he dedicates to the LORD comes from them. Last, wars at Gezer and Gath see their giants killed.
Abraham, also called Abram, descends from Shem through Terah; he fathers Isaac and Ishmael, and later sons including Midian by his concubine Keturah.
Isaac is a son of Abraham and father of Esau and Israel, as listed in 1 Chronicles chapter 1.
Ishmael, a son of Abraham, fathered twelve sons, led by firstborn Nebaioth, then Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam, and others.
Esau, a son of Isaac, fathered Eliphaz, Reuel, Jeush, Jalam, and Korah; the descendants of Eliphaz and Reuel are then listed.

Israel is the people and kingdom of the LORD, described as the offspring of his servant and the children of Jacob, a chosen people made his own forever and redeemed from Egypt. The records present it as a collective that acts largely as a unified body, 'all Israel', whose fortunes are tied to its kings and to its obedience. It is listed by genealogies in the book of the kings of Israel and was the first to resettle its possessions and cities, alongside the priests, Levites and temple servants, while Judah was carried captive to Babylon for disobedience. The account begins with defeat: Israel's men flee the Philistines and fall on Mount Gilboa after Saul and his sons die, and the Israelites abandon their cities to the Philistines. It then turns to unity under David. All Israel gathers at Hebron, calls itself his bone and flesh, and its elders anoint him king according to the LORD's word. Tribes send armed men, Issachar's leaders understand the times, and neighbors bring food amid joy. The assembly agrees to David's plan, and he gathers Israel from the Shihor River of Egypt to the entrance of Hamath, the extent of its bounds. Together they bring the ark to Jerusalem with shouting and music. The LORD establishes David's kingdom, exalted for Israel's sake. Israel's song calls it to remember the covenant and the promised land, and the LORD pledges to appoint it a place, plant it, and no longer let the children of wickedness waste it. Under David, Israel's army led by Joab and Abishai routs the Syrians and Ammonites, and the Syrians make peace and serve David. A shadow falls with the census: Israel counts 1,100,000 swordsmen, Judah 470,000, and God strikes Israel so that seventy thousand die; wrath is also tied to Joab's unfinished census, though the LORD had promised to increase Israel like the stars. The records close with transition and hope. The altar stands for Israel, Solomon's throne is promised forever, and the LORD grants peace and quietness and a land subdued before him. Israel is organized into monthly divisions of twenty-four thousand under tribal rulers. Its leaders are urged to keep all the LORD's commandments so they may possess the good land and leave it to their children forever.

The assembly hears David's appeal and rejoices as the people give willingly. At David's call they bless the LORD, bow down and prostrate themselves before the LORD and the king, and offer sacrifices. They eat and drink with great gladness, make Solomon king a second time, and anoint him, with Zadok as priest.

Edom is a land that had kings before Israel had any, and its chiefs are listed. Later Abishai strikes eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt, garrisons Edom, and all Edomites become David's servants; Edom's silver and gold join spoils dedicated to the LORD.
A succession list of Edom's kings, each reigning in place of the one who died: Bela, Jobab, Husham, Hadad son of Bedad, Samlah, Shaul, Baal Hanan, and finally a later Hadad, whose wife was Mehetabel.

Bela is Benjamin's firstborn son, a head of his father's house. Records list his many sons, including Ezbon, Uzzi, Uzziel, Jerimoth, Iri, Addar, Gera, Abihud, Abishua, Naaman, Ahoah, Shephuphan and Huram.

serves David [Moabites became servants and brought tribute] Moab is defeated by David, and the Moabites become his servants and bring tribute. Silver and gold taken from Moab are among the spoils David dedicates to the LORD.
The chiefs of Edom are eleven listed leaders, named after Hadad died: Timna, Aliah, Jetheth, Oholibamah, Elah, Pinon, Kenaz, Teman, Mibzar, Magdiel, and Iram.

Judah is a man with five sons: Er, Onan and Shelah by Shua's daughter, and Perez and Zerah by his daughter-in-law Tamar. Er, the firstborn, was wicked and killed. Later records list Perez, Hezron, Carmi, Hur and Shobal, tracing many descendant families, including Shelah's line. Judah's children multiplied, unlike the Simeonites' families.
Hezron, a son of Perez, fathered Jerahmeel, Ram, Chelubai and Caleb. At sixty he married Machir's daughter, who bore Segub; after he died, his wife Abijah bore Ashhur, father of Tekoa.
Jerahmeel, Hezron's firstborn and Caleb's brother, fathered Ram and other sons, then with another wife Atarah had Onam; his line extends through Onam's descendants and Sheshan's line.

Caleb is a son of Hezron and brother of Jerahmeel. He married Azubah, then Ephrath after Azubah died, who bore Hur. Jerioth bore Jesher, Shobab and Ardon; concubines Ephah and Maacah bore further sons. His daughter was Achsah; his line through Hur extends to Bethlehem.
Ram is a name borne by two figures: Hezron's son, father of Amminadab and ancestor of David via Nahshon through Jesse; and Jerahmeel's firstborn, father of Maaz, Jamin, Eker.

David is a man, the seventh son of Jesse, with sisters Zeruiah and Abigail, and a member of the house of Judah. He becomes king of Israel, chosen and established by the LORD, and the records follow his rise, reign, and death. Early on he is a fugitive from Saul at Ziklag, where mighty men from many tribes gather to him. After Saul's death the LORD turns the kingdom to him. All Israel gathers at Hebron, where he covenants with the elders and is anointed, in line with the word given through Samuel. He reigns seven years and six months there, then thirty-three years in Jerusalem, taking the stronghold of Zion, which becomes David's city. He grows greater because the LORD of Armies is with him. Hiram sends cedar, masons and carpenters for his house. He becomes famous in all lands, and the nations fear him. His family is large. Six sons are born in Hebron, beginning with Amnon, Daniel, Absalom, Adonijah, Shephatiah and Ithream. In Jerusalem he takes more wives and fathers many more children, including Solomon, Nathan, Shobab, Shammua and others. He also has a daughter, Tamar, and sons by concubines. Religiously, he brings the ark toward Jerusalem. The attempt falters when Uzza is struck, and the ark rests at Obed-Edom's house for a time. He then prepares a tent, insists that Levites carry it, and sets it in the tent. He appoints Levites and singers to serve before it and organizes the priests, Levites and musicians into divisions. Nathan tells him he will not build the LORD a house, but the LORD promises him a great name and a house, and he responds in humble prayer. Militarily, he defeats the Philistines, taking Gath, as well as Moab, Hadadezer of Zobah and the Syrians. He puts garrisons in Damascus, dedicates the spoils to the LORD, and rules with justice and righteousness. He wears the Ammonite king's crown after Rabbah. He sins by ordering a census at Satan's prompting, confesses, and buys Ornan's threshing floor at full price, refusing a sacrifice that costs him nothing. There he builds an altar. In old age he makes Solomon king. He explains that he was barred from building the temple because he was a man of war who shed blood. He gives Solomon the plans, gathers materials, gives his personal treasure, and charges Solomon and the leaders to build. He dies at a good old age, full of days, riches and honor, after reigning forty years. Solomon succeeds him, and his acts are recorded in the histories of Samuel, Nathan and Gad.
Sheshan, son of Ishi and descendant of Jerahmeel, had only daughters. He gave one to his Egyptian servant Jarha, and their son Attai began a line continuing through Nathan to Elishama.
Ethan, son of Kishi, is a Merarite singer who served in the song ministry on the left hand beside Heman and Asaph, with ancestry traced through Abdi, Malluch, Mahli, Mushi, and Merari to Levi.

Heman is a Kohathite singer, son of Joel and descendant of Levi, who served in the song ministry alongside Asaph. Chosen and named with Jeduthun, he gave thanks to the LORD with trumpets and cymbals. Called the king's seer in the words of God, he was given fourteen sons and three daughters, who served under him in song in the LORD's house.

Joab is the son of Zeruiah and brother of Abishai (and Asahel), serving David as captain and commander of the king's army. He first appears going up first against the Jebusites, earning the title of chief as David had promised, and repairing the rest of the city. Later he leads the whole army of mighty men, dividing forces with Abishai, urging courage and trust in the LORD's will; the Syrians flee before him. He then wastes Ammon's country, besieges Rabbah, and overthrows it. When David orders a census, Joab protests, asking why Israel should be made guilty, but the king's word prevails and he carries it out. He reports the totals, omitting Levi and Benjamin because the command was abominable to him. The census is left unfinished, and wrath comes on Israel. He is also the father of Ge Harashim, whose people were craftsmen.

Machir, son of Manasseh and father of Gilead, married Maacah, sister of Huppim and Shuppim. She bore Peresh, whose brother Sheresh continues the line through sons Ulam and Rakem. Gilead's sister was Hammolecheth.

is_a prophet Nathan the prophet first tells David to do all that is in his heart, since God is with him. That night the word of God comes to him, and he faithfully delivers to David the LORD's message and vision, which forbids David to build the house and promises David a house.
Kiriath Jearim, also called Baalah, is a Judah place where the ark stayed in Abinadab's house until David and Israel came to bring it up.
Bethlehem has a Philistine garrison at the time David longs for water from its well by the gate. Elhanan the son of Dodo is listed as being from Bethlehem.

Jabez is a man, more honorable than his brothers, whose mother named him for the sorrow of his birth. He called on Israel's God to bless him, enlarge his border, be with him, and keep him from evil; God granted it.
Group of twelve sons of Israel: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, Dan, Joseph, Benjamin, Naphtali, Gad, Asher; listed in Chapter 2, which then turns to Judah's descendants.

Reuben, firstborn of Israel, defiled his father's couch and so lost his birthright to Joseph's sons; consequently his genealogy isn't listed by birthright, though his sons Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi are named.

Simeon is a patriarchal figure and the name of his descendant clan. His sons were Nemuel, Jamin, Jarib, Zerah, and Shaul. Descent is traced onward through Shallum, Mibsam, and Mishma, with Shimei's large family. The clan did not multiply like Judah, lived in Beersheba, Ziklag and other cities until David's reign, and kept its genealogy.
Levi, father of Gershom, Kohath and Merari, with a troop count of 4600; the singers Heman, Asaph and Ethan trace their genealogies back to him.

Issachar is a figure with four sons, Tola, Puah, Jashub, and Shimron. His families were notable for mighty men of valor, counted by genealogy at 87,000, with army bands of 36,000 due to many wives and sons.
Benjamin is a patriarch who fathered five sons in order: Bela firstborn, Ashbel, Aharah, Nohah, and Rapha. The chapter ends by tracing all listed descendants, including Ulam's archers, to him.
Gad is David's seer who delivers the LORD's offer of three punishments, then relays the angel's command to build an altar on Ornan's threshing floor, which David obeys.

Asher is a patriarch whose sons Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi and Beriah, and sister Serah, begin the line. His descendants become heads of fathers' houses, mighty men of valor, listed by genealogy as 26,000 war-ready fighting men.

The LORD is the God of Israel, presented in these records as a deity who is great and to be feared above all gods, creator of the heavens, good, and whose loving kindness endures forever. He is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, and made an everlasting covenant with them, promising to increase Israel like the stars and giving Canaan as their inheritance. He redeemed Israel out of Egypt and became their God. He searches all hearts, rules over all, and is the source of riches and honor; everything offered for the temple already comes from his hand. The story centers on his transfer of kingship and his establishment of David's line. He killed Saul for trespassing, by not keeping his word and by consulting a familiar spirit instead of inquiring of him, and turned the kingdom to David. He told David he would shepherd Israel, had Samuel anoint him, and gave him victory wherever he went, including against the Philistines, Syria, and Edom. He brought the fear of David on all nations. David dedicated the spoils to him. He is also holy and dangerous. His anger burned against Uzza, who touched the ark, and he struck him dead, yet he blessed Obed-Edom's house while the ark stayed there. He chose the Levites to carry the ark and minister to him forever. When David took a census, he displeased the LORD, who sent a pestilence, relented as the angel was about to destroy Jerusalem, and told the angel to withdraw. He directed an altar at Ornan's threshing floor and answered by fire from the sky. A turning point is his declaration that he has lived in a tent and never asked for a cedar house. He promises David a name, a secure place for Israel, victory over enemies, a house, and an offspring whose throne will be established forever. He has given his people rest and dwells in Jerusalem forever. The records close with succession. He chose David as king, Judah as prince, and Solomon to build the temple, forbidding David to build because of bloodshed. He promises to be Solomon's father and establish his kingdom if Solomon obeys, and he will not fail or forsake Solomon until the work is finished. David praises him as owner of all greatness and the kingdom, the assembly blesses him, and he magnifies Solomon in the sight of all Israel.
